newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: FEATURE - Waistlines, cholesterol haunt Argentine beefeaters.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Waistlines, cholesterol haunt Argentine beefeaters.

text.p: Growing anxiety about expanding waistlines and clogged arteries is beginning to erode Argentines' place as the world's leading beefeaters.

Back in the gluttonous 1960s, Argentines wolfed down a stomach-stretching 200 pounds (90 kg) each every year, man, woman and child. This slipped to about 180 pounds (80 kg) by 1987 and shriveled to a relatively abstemious 123 pounds (56 kg) in 1996, according to the Agriculture Secretariat.

Argentines are on the whole still far from vegetarians and have managed to hold on to the world's joint No. 1 beef-eating spot with their close cousins across the River Plate in Uruguay. But the 1.8 million tonnes of beef Argentina's 35 million people ate in 1996 was 20 percent less than in 1987.

This is cause for concern for the nation's cattlemen, who are pinning their hopes for the future on an export drive. But diet specialists are cheering Argentines along as they try to drag themselves away from their traditionally overladen barbecues, which make the North American variety look austere. Many "parrillas" (barbecue places) offer one-pounder steaks that barely fit on the plate.

All-you-can-eat parrillas, where a waiter places on the table a portable grill filled with all kinds of delicacies such as udder, intestines, blood sausages, salivary glands, kidneys and ribs, are also very popular.

"We specialists are aiming at a change in consumption habits," said Paula Busquelli, a nutritionist for the Cormilloc Clinic in Buenos Aires. "The recommendation is only to eat about 750 grams (1.7 lb) of red meat a week, over two or three days."
ARGENTINES SPOOKED BY CHOLESTEROL

While defending beef as a source of iron, Busquelli said the specter of cholesterol clogging up their bloodstreams was beginning to spook carnivorous Argentines. "Lean meat isn't bad for your health but gives you the proteins your body needs and they are not as harmful as some cheeses," she said.

But something is in the air and it is not the smell of beef, which usually wafts around Buenos Aires at lunchtime. Office workers, long accustomed to lunch on a thick steak or greasy wiener schnitzel, are increasingly venturing into an uncharted "lite" territory of salads, soybean stews, and mineral water.
"Now we eat salads and low-fat foods so as not to get fat, and also for money reasons -- it's cheaper," government worker Mario Beridian said.
While dishes alleged to be "salads" in Argentina are often packed with chicken, cheese or hard-boiled eggs, the younger generation is increasingly prepared to go without any meat.

Beef has always been the basis of the Argentine diet. The English naturalist Charles Darwin complained of the lack of vegetables in Argentina during his voyage in the Beagle back in the 1830s. And Argentine folklore is based on beef, with the principal character being the tough "gaucho" cowboy, as quick to pull a knife on a foe as to use it to slice his steak.
CHICKEN UP, BEEF DOWN

"The fall in red meat consumption is part of a general change in eating patterns where chicken consumption, and to a lesser degree fish consumption, have risen," cattle industry analyst Guillermo Vieytes said.
Argentines are now tucking into 40 pounds (18 kg) of chicken each a year but still only 6 pounds (2.7 kg) of fish.
"Dietary habits are very deeply ingrained, it's a cultural thing," Busquelli said. "Not everyone is used to the taste of fish in their daily diet."

Ironically, just as Argentines are steering away from beef in search of lower cholesterol levels, their beef is being marketed abroad as lower in fat than its competitors. The government claims that having room to roam around the Pampa grasslands keeps Argentine cattle leaner than its more sedentary American cousins, cooped up in pens chowing on man-made food.

Exports soared to about 510,000 tonnes in 1995 but sagged last year to around 470,000 tonnes as the world beef trade was battered by the "mad cow" scare. The Argentine export offensive is made possible by its victory over foot-and-mouth disease, which long kept it locked out of big premium-priced markets.
Argentina scored a key victory recently when U.S. officials gave assurances they would soon officially announce sanitary approval for a 20,000-tonne annual import quota.
The government hopes exports will double to one million tonnes a year by the end of the century, although many in the industry privately consider that figure overly optimistic.
